On the global existence and uniform-in-time bounds for three-component reaction-diffusion systems with mass control and polynomial growth

Journal: Journal of Differential Equations
Redouane Douaifiaa,b, Salem Abdelmalekc, Mokhtar Kiraned,∗ Address: (a) Process Engineering Department, Faculty of Technology, University of Blida 1, Blida, Algeria
(b) Water Environment and Sustainable Development Laboratory, Faculty of Technology, Blida 1 University, PO Box 270-09000, Blida, Algeria
(c) Department of Mathematics, Laboratory (LAMIS), Echahid Cheikh Larbi Tebessi University, Tebessa, Algeria
(d) Department of Mathematics, College of Computing and Mathematical Sciences, Khalifa University, P.O. Box: 127788, Abu Dhabi, UAE
(*) Corresponding author, email: mokhtar.kirane@ku.ac.ae
Abstract

We investigate a class of three-component reaction–diffusion systems subject to mass control and a newly introduced structural assumption, referred to as linear intermediate weighted sum condition. Under these hypotheses, we establish the global existence of classical solutions in arbitrary spatial dimensions and wide class of boundary conditions, even when the nonlinearities exhibit arbitrary polynomial growth. We establish also that, under slight-stronger assumptions and mixed boundary conditions, solutions admit uniform-in-time bounds. Our approach relies on the extension of LpL^{p}-energy polynomial functionals, together with the regularizing effect for parabolic equations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our framework by analyzing three-species sub-skew-symmetric Lotka–Volterra systems with higher-order interactions.

Keywords: 
Reaction-diffusion systems; mass control; linear intermediate weighted sum; polynomial growth; global existence; LpL^{p}-energy polynomial functionals; three-species Lotka-Voltera model; higher order interactions.

1 Introduction

This work examines the global existence of classical solutions for a class of semilinear reaction-diffusion systems consisting of three equations.

1.1 Problem setting

Let N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, and Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} is a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. We consider the reaction-diffusion system.

{∂u∂t−d1​Δ​u=f⁡(u,v,w),in ​Ω×(0,+∞),∂v∂t−d2​Δ​v=g⁡(u,v,w),in ​Ω×(0,+∞),∂w∂t−d3​Δ​w=h⁡(u,v,w),in ​Ω×(0,+∞),∂u∂η​(x,t)=∂v∂η​(x,t)=∂w∂η​(x,t)=0,on ​∂Ω×(0,+∞),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)​, ​v​(x,0)=v0​(x)​, ​w​(x,0)=w0​(x),in ​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}-d_{1}\Delta u=f\left(u,v,w\right),&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}-d_{2}\Delta v=g\left(u,v,w\right),&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial w}{\partial t}-d_{3}\Delta w=h\left(u,v,w\right),&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=\frac{\partial w}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=0,&\text{on }\partial\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \\ u\left(x,0\right)=u_{0}(x)\text{, }v\left(x,0\right)=v_{0}(x)\text{, }w\left(x,0\right)=w_{0}(x),&\text{in }\Omega,\end{array}\right. (1.1)

where d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0 are diffusion coefficients, η\eta is the unit outward normal vector on ∂Ω\partial\Omega, u0u_{0}, v0v_{0}, and w0w_{0} are initial data. Under the notations ξ=(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)\xi=(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3}) and Λ⁡(ξ)=1+ξ1+ξ2+ξ3\Lambda(\xi)=1+\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}+\xi_{3}, the following assumptions are made regarding the nonlinearities:

  1. (𝒜\mathcal{A}1)

    (Quasi-positivity and Local Lipschitz) The nonlinearities f,g,h:ℝ3⟶ℝf,g,h:\mathbb{R}^{3}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} are locally Lipschitz, and

    f⁡(0,ξ2,ξ3),g⁡(ξ1,0,ξ3),h⁡(ξ1,ξ2,0)≥0, for any ​ξ∈ℝ+3.f\left(0,\xi_{2},\xi_{3}\right),g\left(\xi_{1},0,\xi_{3}\right),h\left(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},0\right)\geq 0,\ \text{ for any }\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}. (1.2)
  2. (𝒜\mathcal{A}2)

    (Mass Control) There exists K1≥0K_{1}\geq 0, such that

    f⁡(ξ)+g⁡(ξ)+h⁡(ξ)≤K1​Λ​(ξ), for any ​ξ∈ℝ+3.f\left(\xi\right)+g\left(\xi\right)+h\left(\xi\right)\leq K_{1}\Lambda(\xi),\ \text{ for any }\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}. (1.3)
  3. (𝒜\mathcal{A}3)

    (Linear Intermediate Weighted Sum) There exist Ki≥0K_{i}\geq 0 for i=2,3,4i=2,3,4, and λ1,λ2>1\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>1 (or λ1,λ2<1\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}<1), such that

    {λ1​f​(ξ)+g⁡(ξ)+h⁡(ξ)≤K2​Λ​(ξ),λ2​f​(ξ)+λ2​g​(ξ)+h⁡(ξ)≤K3​Λ​(ξ),λ1​λ2​f​(ξ)+λ2​g​(ξ)+h⁡(ξ)≤K4​Λ​(ξ),\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}\lambda_{1}f\left(\xi\right)+g\left(\xi\right)+h\left(\xi\right)\leq K_{2}\Lambda(\xi),\\ \\ \lambda_{2}f\left(\xi\right)+\lambda_{2}g\left(\xi\right)+h\left(\xi\right)\leq K_{3}\Lambda(\xi),\\ \\ \lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}f\left(\xi\right)+\lambda_{2}g\left(\xi\right)+h\left(\xi\right)\leq K_{4}\Lambda(\xi),\end{array}\right. (1.4)

    for any ξ∈ℝ+3.\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}.

  4. (𝒜\mathcal{A}4)

    (Polynomial Growth) There exist m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} and M>0M>0, such that

    f⁡(ξ),g⁡(ξ),h⁡(ξ)≤M​(Λ⁡(ξ))m,for any ​ξ∈ℝ+3.f\left(\xi\right),g\left(\xi\right),h\left(\xi\right)\leq M(\Lambda(\xi))^{m},\ \text{for any }\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}. (1.5)

We now turn to a discussion of the structural assumptions ( A 1)-( A 4). Assumption ( A 1), which requires quasi-positivity together with local Lipschitz continuity, is classical in the analysis of reaction–diffusion systems. These conditions guarantee local existence of solutions and, importantly, ensure their non-negativity, i.e. the invariance of the positive octant under the flow. The latter property is particularly relevant for systems arising in biology or chemistry, since it preserves the physical meaning of the model: if the initial concentration (or density, or population) is non-negative, then the corresponding solution remains non-negative throughout its evolution. Assumption ( A 2) serves as a unifying framework that extends several classical hypotheses commonly used in the literature, in particular:

  • •

    mass conservation:

    f⁡(ξ)+g⁡(ξ)+h⁡(ξ)=0, for any ​ξ∈ℝ+3.f\left(\xi\right)+g\left(\xi\right)+h\left(\xi\right)=0,\ \text{ for any }\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}. (1.6)
  • •

    mass dissipation:

    f⁡(ξ)+g⁡(ξ)+h⁡(ξ)≤0, for any ​ξ∈ℝ+3.f\left(\xi\right)+g\left(\xi\right)+h\left(\xi\right)\leq 0,\ \text{ for any }\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}. (1.7)

The assumption ( A 3) that we have called "intermediate wheighted sum condition (IWSC)", which is a modefied version of the so-called "intermediate sum condition (ISC)":
There exist an 3×33\times 3 lower triangle matrix A=(ai​j)A=(a_{ij}) with nonnegative elements and ai​i>0a_{ii}>0 for all i=1,2,3i=1,2,3, a constant r≥1r\geq 1 and a constant K>0K>0, such that

{a11​f​(ξ)≤K​Λr​(ξ),a21​f​(ξ)+a22​g​(ξ)≤K​Λr​(ξ),a31​f​(ξ)+a32​g​(ξ)+a33​h​(ξ)≤K​Λr​(ξ),\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}a_{11}f\left(\xi\right)\leq K\Lambda^{r}(\xi),\\ \\ a_{21}f\left(\xi\right)+a_{22}g\left(\xi\right)\leq K\Lambda^{r}(\xi),\\ \\ a_{31}f\left(\xi\right)+a_{32}g\left(\xi\right)+a_{33}h\left(\xi\right)\leq K\Lambda^{r}(\xi),\end{array}\right. (1.8)

for any ξ∈ℝ+3.\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}. The essential difference between these conditions is that, in (ISC) one of the nonlinearties is assumed to be upper bounded by a polynomial of order rr (in particular less than 1+2N1+\frac{2}{N}, or, for small dimension, rr is at most 33), while in (IWSC), we need three wheighted sum of all nonlinearties. Assumption ( A 4) requires that the nonlinearities exhibit at most polynomial growth of order mm. It is worth emphasizing that the results established in this paper impose no restriction on the value of mm.

1.2 State of the art and motivation

The investigation of global existence for reaction-diffusion systems has attracted continuous attention for last decades as a fundamental question. Despite being a classical subject, it remains a source of numerous open questions and mathematical challenges, even in systems that look simple and are based on real-world uses, such reversible chemical processes. A major difficulty arises from the fact that, reaction-diffusion systems generally (consisting of two or more equations) lack a maximum principle or invariant regions, often nonlinearities have not a constant sign and this means that the local solution is a priori bounded or at least bounded in some LpL^{p}-space. Early contributions to this topic include the works of Alikakos [5], Haraux and Kirane [15], Masuda [24], Rothe [32], Amann [6], Hollis, Martin, and Pierre [18], Haraux and Youkana [16], Morgan [25], Kouachi [21, 22], as well as Abdelmalek and Kouachi [1].

It is well known that assumptions ( A 1) and ( A 2) by themselves do not exclude the possibility of finite-time blow-up of solutions to system (1.1); see [28]. This observation naturally led to an intensive study of systems supplemented by additional structural conditions, in particular ( A 4). Some advance were obtained by [14, 7, 9, 30, 26], where, under the entropy inequality or without, global existence of bounded solutions was established with specific assumptions, for instance, small space dimensions (N=1,2N=1,2) and at most cubic systems or strictly sub-quadratic systems in all dimensions. The global existence of quadratic systems in higher dimensions remained unresolved until a series of contributions [33, 8, 12] closed this gap. In the first two, the entropy inequality continued to play a role, whereas the last one succeeded in removing this requirement. Moreover, Fellner et al., complemented the analysis in [13] by establishing the uniform boundedness in time of solutions. It is worth noting that most of the previous works dealt with systems that impose homogeneous conditions (Neumann and/or Dirichlet), but some of them dealt with non-homogeneous boundary conditions as in [25, 19, 22, 1]. For more details we refer the reader to the surveys [29, 31].

The results summarized above indicate that global existence together with uniform-in-time bounds for nonnegative classical solutions can be ensured either in the presence of quadratic nonlinearities (or super-quadratic ones subject to dimension constraints), or under structural conditions of the form (1.8). However, such conditions are not generally satisfied by a wide class of systems. To illustrate this limitation, we consider the following nonlinearities:

{f⁡(ξ)=ξ25−ξ16,g⁡(ξ)=ξ37−B​ξ25,h⁡(ξ)=ξ16−C​ξ37,\left\{\begin{aligned} f(\xi)&=\xi_{2}^{5}-\xi_{1}^{6},\\ g(\xi)&=\xi_{3}^{7}-B\xi_{2}^{5},\\ h(\xi)&=\xi_{1}^{6}-C\xi_{3}^{7},\end{aligned}\right. (1.9)

where BB and CC are positive constants chosen sufficiently large. It is clear that the nonlinearities (1.9) do not satisfy the so-called linear intermediate sum condition (1.8), as well as are not quadratic. Nevertheless, it can be verified that the nonlinearities (1.9) satisfy our proposed condition, referred to as the linear intermediate weighted sum (1.4), by an appropriate choice of the parameters BB and CC. This observation constitutes a central motivation of the present work. Specifically, by employing the linear intermediate weighted sum condition ( A 3), we are able to accommodate nonlinearities with arbitrary polynomial growth. A natural question then arises: can one establish uniform-in-time bounds for solutions of (1.1) subject to mixed boundary conditions under assumptions ( A 1)-( A 4)? We give a positive answer to this issue in this work.

Assume the conditions ( A 1), ( A 2), ( A 3) for some λ1≤\lambda_{1}\leq θ−2​p\theta^{-2p}, λ2≤\lambda_{2}\leq σ−2​p\sigma^{-2p}, and ( A 4) where the assumptions (1.10), (1.11) are fulfilled, and u0,v0,w0∈L∞​(Ω,ℝ+)u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}\in L^{\infty}\left(\Omega;\mathbb{R}_{+}\right). 1.4 Structure of the paper

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 is devoted to the proofs of the main results; Subsection 2.1 recalls some preliminaries, Subsection 2.2 establishes the global existence of solutions in Theorem 1, Subsection 2.3 derives the uniform-in-time bounds associated with Theorem 1, Subsection 2.4 provides the proof of Theorem 2, and Subsection 2.5 presents the generalizations leading to the proofs of Theorems 3 and 4. Section 3 discusses applications of the results to specific models; Example 1 is treated in Subsection 3.1, Example 2 in Subsection 3.2, and Example 3 of three-species sub-skew-symmetric Lotka–Volterra systems with higher-order interactions, in Subsection 3.3.

2 Proof of main results

2.1 Preliminaries

We start with the definition of classical solutions.

Definition 1 (Classical solutions).

Let 0<T≤∞0<T\leq\infty. A classical solution to (1.13) on (0,T)(0,T) is a vector of functions S:=(u,v,w)S:=(u,v,w), satisfying u,v,w∈C⁡([0,T],Lp​(Ω))∩L∞​(Ω×(0,T))∩C1,2​(Ω¯×(τ,T))u,v,w\in C([0,T];L^{p}(\Omega))\cap L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T))\cap C^{1,2}(\overline{\Omega}\times(\tau,T)) for all p>1p>1 and all 0<τ<T0<\tau<T, and SS satisfies each equation in (1.13) pointwise in Ω×(0,T)\Omega\times(0,T).

According to assumption ( A 1), it is a classical task to show the existence of a unique local nonnegative classical solution of system (1.1) on [0,Tm​a​x)[0,T_{max}), where Tm​a​xT_{max} is the eventual blow-up time in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}\left(\Omega\right) (see e.g. [17, 32]).

Proposition 1.

Suppose that u0,v0,w0∈L∞​(Ω,ℝ+)u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}\in L^{\infty}\left(\Omega;\mathbb{R}_{+}\right) and ( A 1) holds. Then there exists Tm​a​x>0T_{max}>0 such that (1.1) admits a unique nonnegative classical solution on [0,Tm​a​x)[0,T_{max}). Moreover, if Tm​a​x<+∞T_{max}<+\infty, then

lim supt→Tm​a​x−(‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω))=+∞.\limsup_{t\rightarrow T_{max}^{-}}\left(\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|w(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\right)=+\infty.

It is essential to first establish the following lemmas.

Lemma 1.

Let Φ⁡(ξ),Ψ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi),\Psi(\xi) be two real-valued functions defined on ℝ+3\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}, α>1\alpha>1 (or 0<α<10<\alpha<1), and C1,C2≥0C_{1},C_{2}\geq 0. Then, for all ξ∈ℝ+3\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}, we have

implies

α∗​Φ​(ξ)+Ψ⁡(ξ)≤max⁡{C1,C2}​Λ​(ξ),\alpha^{\ast}\Phi(\xi)+\Psi(\xi)\leq\max\left\{C_{1},C_{2}\right\}\Lambda(\xi),

for all α∗∈[1,α]\alpha^{\ast}\in[1,\alpha] (or for all α∗∈[α,1]\alpha^{\ast}\in[\alpha,1]).

The proof is by contradiction. Let ξ∈ℝ+3\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}, and there exists α∗∈[1,α]\alpha^{\ast}\in[1,\alpha], such that

{Φ⁡(ξ)+Ψ⁡(ξ)≤C1​Λ​(ξ),andα​Φ​(ξ)+Ψ⁡(ξ)≤C2​Λ​(ξ),\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}\Phi(\xi)+\Psi(\xi)\leq C_{1}\Lambda(\xi),\\ \text{and}\\ \alpha\Phi(\xi)+\Psi(\xi)\leq C_{2}\Lambda(\xi),\end{array}\right.

and

This leads to a contradiction. For the case α∗∈(α,1)\alpha^{\ast}\in(\alpha,1), we obtain

{(1−α∗)​Φ​(ξ)<0​ implies ​Φ​(ξ)<0,and(α−α∗)​Φ​(ξ)<0​ implies ​Φ​(ξ)>0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}(1-\alpha^{\ast})\Phi(\xi)<0\text{ implies }\Phi(\xi)<0,\\ \text{and}\\ (\alpha-\alpha^{\ast})\Phi(\xi)<0\text{ implies }\Phi(\xi)>0.\end{array}\right.

2.3 Theorem 1: Uniform-in-time bounds

We first show that for any 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty, there exists a constant Cp>0C_{p}>0 such that

supt≥0∥u(.,t)∥Lp​(Ω),supt≥0∥v(.,t)∥Lp​(Ω),supt≥0∥w(.,t)∥Lp​(Ω)≤Cp.\sup_{t\geq 0}\|u(.,t)\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)},\sup_{t\geq 0}\|v(.,t)\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)},\sup_{t\geq 0}\|w(.,t)\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\leq C_{p}. (2.12)

Indeed, by employing the LpL^{p}-energy function ℒ⁡(t)\mathcal{L}(t) together with ℒ~​(t)=(θ​σ)p​ℒ​(t)\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(t)=(\theta\sigma)^{p}\mathcal{L}(t), and carrying out computations analogous to those in Proposition 2, while taking into account the assumptions ( A 2) and ( A 3) with Ki=0K_{i}=0, for all i=1,…,4i=1,\dots,4, we obtain

ℒ~′​(t)≤0.\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}^{\prime}(t)\leq 0. (2.13)

Thus, there exists a positive constant C^\widehat{C}, such that

supt≥0ℒ⁡(t)≤C^.\sup_{t\geq 0}\mathcal{L}(t)\leq\widehat{C}.

Hence, we get (2.12). To finally see that the solution is bounded uniformly in time in sup norm, we use a smooth cut-off function ψ:ℝ→[0,1]\psi:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1] with ψ⁡(s)=0\psi(s)=0 for s≤0s\leq 0 and ψ⁡(s)=1\psi(s)=1 for s≥1s\geq 1, 0≤ψ′≤M0\leq\psi^{\prime}\leq M, with M>0M>0, and its shifted version ψτ(⋅)=ψ(⋅−τ)\psi_{\tau}(\cdot)=\psi(\cdot-\tau) for any τ∈ℕ\tau\in\mathbb{N}. Let τ∈ℕ\tau\in\mathbb{N} be arbitrary. By multiplying the system (1.1) by ψτ\psi_{\tau}, we obtain

{∂(ψτ​u)∂t−d1​Δ​(ψτ​u)=ψτ′​u+ψτ​f​(u,v,w),in ​Ω×(τ,τ+ρ),∂(ψτ​v)∂t−d2​Δ​(ψτ​v)=ψτ′​v+ψτ​g​(u,v,w),in ​Ω×(τ,τ+ρ),∂(ψτ​w)∂t−d3​Δ​(ψτ​w)=ψτ′​w+ψτ​h​(u,v,w),in ​Ω×(τ,τ+ρ),∂(ψτ​u)∂η​(x,t)=∂(ψτ​v)∂η​(x,t)=∂(ψτ​w)∂η​(x,t)=0,on ​∂Ω×(τ,τ+ρ),(ψτ​u)​(x,τ)=(ψτ​v)​(x,τ)=(ψτ​w)​(x,τ)=0,in ​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\displaystyle\frac{\partial(\psi_{\tau}u)}{\partial t}-d_{1}\Delta(\psi_{\tau}u)=\psi_{\tau}^{\prime}u+\psi_{\tau}f\left(u,v,w\right),&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(\tau,\tau+\rho\right),\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial(\psi_{\tau}v)}{\partial t}-d_{2}\Delta(\psi_{\tau}v)=\psi_{\tau}^{\prime}v+\psi_{\tau}g\left(u,v,w\right),&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(\tau,\tau+\rho\right),\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial(\psi_{\tau}w)}{\partial t}-d_{3}\Delta(\psi_{\tau}w)=\psi_{\tau}^{\prime}w+\psi_{\tau}h\left(u,v,w\right),&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(\tau,\tau+\rho\right),\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial(\psi_{\tau}u)}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=\frac{\partial(\psi_{\tau}v)}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=\frac{\partial(\psi_{\tau}w)}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=0,&\text{on }\partial\Omega\times\left(\tau,\tau+\rho\right),\\ \\ (\psi_{\tau}u)\left(x,\tau\right)=(\psi_{\tau}v)\left(x,\tau\right)=(\psi_{\tau}w)\left(x,\tau\right)=0,&\text{in }\Omega,\end{array}\right. Proof of Theorem 4.

ℒ~1′​(t)=ℐ∗+ℐ^∗+𝒥∗,\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{1}^{\prime}(t)=\mathcal{I}^{\ast}+\widehat{\mathcal{I}}^{\ast}+\mathcal{J}^{\ast}, (2.22)

3.1 Example 1

Consider the example:

{∂u∂t−d1​Δ​u=vl−uq,in ​Ω×(0,+∞),∂v∂t−d2​Δ​v=wr−B​vl,in ​Ω×(0,+∞),∂w∂t−d3​Δ​w=A​uq−C​wr,in ​Ω×(0,+∞),∂u∂η​(x,t)=∂v∂η​(x,t)=∂w∂η​(x,t)=0,on ​∂Ω×(0,+∞),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)​, ​v​(x,0)=v0​(x)​, ​w​(x,0)=w0​(x),in ​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}-d_{1}\Delta u=v^{l}-u^{q},&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}-d_{2}\Delta v=w^{r}-Bv^{l},&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial w}{\partial t}-d_{3}\Delta w=Au^{q}-Cw^{r},&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=\frac{\partial w}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=0,&\text{on }\partial\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \\ u\left(x,0\right)=u_{0}(x)\text{, }v\left(x,0\right)=v_{0}(x)\text{, }w\left(x,0\right)=w_{0}(x),&\text{in }\Omega,\end{array}\right. Let A≤1A\leq 1, B≥θ2​(p−1)B\geq\theta^{2(p-1)}, C≥σ2​(p−1)C\geq\sigma^{2(p-1)}, such that p>(N+2)2max{l.q.r}p>\frac{\left(N+2\right)}{2}\max\{l.q.r\}, and θ,σ\theta,\sigma satisfy (1.10)\left(\text{\ref{Teta_Sigma_Conds}}\right). supt≥0∥u(.,t)∥L∞​(Ω),supt≥0∥v(.,t)∥L∞​(Ω),supt≥0∥w(.,t)∥L∞​(Ω)<+∞.\sup_{t\geq 0}\|u(.,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\quad\sup_{t\geq 0}\|v(.,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\quad\sup_{t\geq 0}\|w(.,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<+\infty. (3.2)

As all the assumptions of Theorem 1 are fulfilled. Then, the global existence and uniform boundedness in time of the solution to system (3.1)\left(\text{\ref{Sys_Ex1}}\right) follows directly. ∎

We have the following result.

Theorem 6.

According to the assumptions (3.5)\left(\text{\ref{Cond1_Ex2}}\right)-(3.9)\left(\text{\ref{Cond5_Ex2}}\right) where (1.10)\left(\text{\ref{Teta_Sigma_Conds}}\right) holds, and for any u0,v0,w0∈L∞​(Ω,ℝ+)u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}\in L^{\infty}\left(\Omega;\mathbb{R}_{+}\right), there exists a unique nonnegative global classical solution to the system (3.3). Moreover, the solution is bounded uniformly in time, i.e.

supt≥0∥u(.,t)∥L∞​(Ω),supt≥0∥v(.,t)∥L∞​(Ω),supt≥0∥w(.,t)∥L∞​(Ω)<+∞.\sup_{t\geq 0}\|u(.,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\quad\sup_{t\geq 0}\|v(.,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\quad\sup_{t\geq 0}\|w(.,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<+\infty. (3.10)
Proof.

The reaction functions (3.4)\left(\text{\ref{ReacFuncs_Ex2}}\right), under the conditions (3.5)\left(\text{\ref{Cond1_Ex2}}\right)-(3.9)\left(\text{\ref{Cond5_Ex2}}\right), can be readily verified to satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 1. Consequently, the global existence and uniform boundedness in time of the solution to system (3.3)\left(\text{\ref{Sys_Ex2}}\right) are established. ∎

3.3 Example 3: HOIs three-species Lotka-Voltera model

In contrast to the previous examples, where the parameters of the systems are dependent on the spatial dimension, the growth polynomial’s order, and the diffusion coefficients, the current example admits parameters that remain independent of these quantities. A direct application of Theorems 3 and 4 demonstrates the existence of global classical solution in arbitrary spatial dimensions for nonlinear three-species sub-skew-symmetric Lotka-Volterra involving higher order interactions and linear diffusion, expressed in the following form:

{∂u∂t−d1​Δ​u=τ1​u+uγ1​(a11​uγ1+a12​vγ2+a13​wγ3),in ​Ω×(0,+∞),∂v∂t−d2​Δ​v=τ2​v+vγ2​(a21​uγ1+a22​vγ2+a23​wγ3),in ​Ω×(0,+∞),∂w∂t−d3​Δ​w=τ3​w+wγ3​(a31​uγ1+a32​vγ2+a33​wγ3),in ​Ω×(0,+∞),λ1​u​(x,t)+(1−λ1)​∂u∂η​(x,t)=β1,λ2​v​(x,t)+(1−λ2)​∂v∂η​(x,t)=β2,λ3​w​(x,t)+(1−λ3)​∂w∂η​(x,t)=β3,on ​∂Ω×(0,+∞),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)​, ​v​(x,0)=v0​(x)​, ​w​(x,0)=w0​(x),in ​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\vskip 5.69046pt\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}-d_{1}\Delta u=\tau_{1}u+u^{\gamma_{1}}\left(a_{11}u^{\gamma_{1}}+a_{12}v^{\gamma_{2}}+a_{13}w^{\gamma_{3}}\right),&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \vskip 5.69046pt\displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}-d_{2}\Delta v=\tau_{2}v+v^{\gamma_{2}}\left(a_{21}u^{\gamma_{1}}+a_{22}v^{\gamma_{2}}+a_{23}w^{\gamma_{3}}\right),&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial w}{\partial t}-d_{3}\Delta w=\tau_{3}w+w^{\gamma_{3}}\left(a_{31}u^{\gamma_{1}}+a_{32}v^{\gamma_{2}}+a_{33}w^{\gamma_{3}}\right),&\text{in }\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ \begin{array}[]{c}\displaystyle\lambda_{1}u(x,t)+\left(1-\lambda_{1}\right)\frac{\partial u}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=\beta_{1},\\ \displaystyle\lambda_{2}v(x,t)+\left(1-\lambda_{2}\right)\frac{\partial v}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=\beta_{2},\\ \displaystyle\lambda_{3}w(x,t)+\left(1-\lambda_{3}\right)\frac{\partial w}{\partial\eta}\left(x,t\right)=\beta_{3},\end{array}&\text{on }\partial\Omega\times\left(0,+\infty\right),\\ u\left(x,0\right)=u_{0}(x)\text{, }v\left(x,0\right)=v_{0}(x)\text{, }w\left(x,0\right)=w_{0}(x),&\text{in }\Omega,\end{array}\right. (3.11)

where A=(ai​j)∈ℝ3×3A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} is sub-skew-symmetric matrix, i.e. A+AT≤0A+A^{T}\leq 0 where all elements of A+ATA+A^{T} are non-positive, (τ1,τ2,τ3)∈ℝ3(\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, and γi≥1\gamma_{i}\geq 1 for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3. The boundary conditions are defined as (1.14)-(1.17).

The diffusive Lotka-Volterra model with higher order interactions (3.11)\left(\text{\ref{3SHOIs_LV}}\right), is inspired by the works [3, 4, 10, 11, 34, 36]. The model (3.11)\left(\text{\ref{3SHOIs_LV}}\right) with γi=1\gamma_{i}=1 for i=1.2.3i=1.2.3, and homogeneous Neumann or Dirichlet boundary conditions, have been extensively investigated in the literature due to their wide application in biology, see e.g. [17, 30, 32, 35]. All the previous mentioned works concern either weak solutions in all space dimensions or classical solutions in small (one and two) space dimensions. Until recently, Fellner et al. [12, 13] dealt with the case of skew-symmetric Lotka-Volterra systems (i.e. A+AT=0A+A^{T}=0) with m−m-equations and 2≤m∈ℕ2\leq m\in\mathbb{N}, their results imply the existence of classical solution in all space dimensions. It is worth noting that their results cannot guarantee the global existence of solutions to the system (3.11)\left(\text{\ref{3SHOIs_LV}}\right) with nonhomogeneous Robin boundary conditions, even at least for γi=1\gamma_{i}=1, for i=1.2.3i=1.2.3. The outcomes of our study ensure the global existence of classical solutions of a class of (3.11)\left(\text{\ref{3SHOIs_LV}}\right), where these systems hold for a wide range of boundary conditions (1.14)\left(\text{\ref{HNBCs_EX3}}\right)-(1.17)\left(\text{\ref{MixNHRBCsHDBCs_EX3}}\right), and γi≥1\gamma_{i}\geq 1 for i=1.2.3i=1.2.3. In order to simplify the notations, we define

𝒮​𝒦3×3={A=(ai​j)1≤i,j≤3∈ℝ3×3:A+AT≤0},\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}=\left\{A=(a_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq 3}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}\ :\ A+A^{T}\leq 0\right\},
𝒮𝒦3×3+={A∈𝒮𝒦3×3: ai​j≥0 with i<j, for i,j=1,2,3},\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{+}=\left\{A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}:\text{ }a_{ij}\geq 0\text{ with }i<j\text{, for }i,j=1,2,3\right\},

and

𝒮𝒦3×3−={A∈𝒮𝒦3×3:ai​j≤0 with i<j, for i,j=1,2,3}.\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{-}=\left\{A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}:a_{ij}\leq 0\text{ with }i<j\text{, for }i,j=1,2,3\right\}.

By employing our aforementioned approach, we can deduce the following result.

Theorem 7 (HOIs 3-species Lotka-Voltera model).

Let N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, and Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} is a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, where τi∈ℝ\tau_{i}\in\mathbb{R}, and γi≥1\gamma_{i}\geq 1 for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3. Additionally, let A∈𝒮​𝒦3×3−A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{-} or A∈𝒮​𝒦3×3+A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{+}. Then for any non-negative initial conditions u0,v0,w0∈L∞​(Ω)u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}\in L^{\infty}\left(\Omega\right), and when one of the boundary conditions (1.14)\left(\text{\ref{HNBCs_EX3}}\right)-(1.17)\left(\text{\ref{MixNHRBCsHDBCs_EX3}}\right) is imposed, there exists a unique nonnegative global classical solution to (3.11)\left(\text{\ref{3SHOIs_LV}}\right). Moreover, if τi≤0\tau_{i}\leq 0 for all i=1,2,3i=1,2,3 and in (1.16) or (1.17) we have βi≡0\beta_{i}\equiv 0 for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3, then the solution is bounded uniformly in time, i.e.

supt≥0∥u(.,t)∥L∞​(Ω),supt≥0∥v(.,t)∥L∞​(Ω),supt≥0∥w(.,t)∥L∞​(Ω)<+∞.\sup_{t\geq 0}\|u(.,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\quad\sup_{t\geq 0}\|v(.,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\quad\sup_{t\geq 0}\|w(.,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<+\infty. (3.12)
Proof.

Set

{f~​(S):=uγ1​(a11​uγ1+a12​vγ2+a13​wγ3),g~​(S):=vγ2​(a21​uγ1+a22​vγ2+a23​wγ3),h~​(S):=wγ3​(a31​uγ1+a32​vγ2+a33​wγ3),\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}\widetilde{f}(S):=u^{\gamma_{1}}\left(a_{11}u^{\gamma_{1}}+a_{12}v^{\gamma_{2}}+a_{13}w^{\gamma_{3}}\right),\\ \widetilde{g}(S):=v^{\gamma_{2}}\left(a_{21}u^{\gamma_{1}}+a_{22}v^{\gamma_{2}}+a_{23}w^{\gamma_{3}}\right),\\ \widetilde{h}(S):=w^{\gamma_{3}}\left(a_{31}u^{\gamma_{1}}+a_{32}v^{\gamma_{2}}+a_{33}w^{\gamma_{3}}\right),\end{array}\right. (3.13)

and

{𝒞~1​(S):=λ1​f~​(S)+g~​(S)+h~​(S),𝒞~2​(S):=λ2​f~​(S)+λ2​g~​(S)+h~​(S),𝒞~3​(S):=λ1​λ2​f​(S)+λ2​g​(S)+h⁡(S).\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{1}(S):=\lambda_{1}\widetilde{f}(S)+\widetilde{g}(S)+\widetilde{h}(S),\\ \widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{2}(S):=\lambda_{2}\widetilde{f}(S)+\lambda_{2}\widetilde{g}(S)+\widetilde{h}(S),\\ \widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{3}(S):=\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}f(S)+\lambda_{2}g(S)+h(S).\end{array}\right.

The verification of the assumptions ( A 1) and ( A 4) is straightforward. Since A∈𝒮​𝒦3×3−⊂𝒮​𝒦A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{-}\subset\mathcal{SK} or A∈𝒮​𝒦3×3+⊂𝒮​𝒦A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{+}\subset\mathcal{SK}, thus the assumption ( A 2) is easily obtained. Now, by substituting (3.13)\left(\text{\ref{RFs_EX3proof}}\right) into the left-hand side of the inequalities (1.4)\left(\text{\ref{EqCond_a3}}\right), we get

{𝒞~1​(S)≤(λ1​a12+a21)​uγ1​vγ2+(λ1​a13+a31)​uγ1​wγ3,𝒞~2​(S)≤(λ2​a13+a31)​uγ1​wγ3+(λ2​a23+a32)​vγ2​wγ3,𝒞~3​(S)≤(λ1​λ2​a13+a31)​uγ1​wγ3+(λ1​a12+a21)​uγ1​vγ2​λ2+(λ2​a23+a32)​vγ2​wγ3.\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{1}(S)\leq\left(\allowbreak\lambda_{1}a_{12}+a_{21}\right)u^{\gamma_{1}}v^{\gamma_{2}}+\left(\allowbreak\lambda_{1}a_{13}+a_{31}\right)u^{\gamma_{1}}w^{\gamma_{3}},\\ \widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{2}(S)\leq\left(\lambda_{2}a_{13}+\allowbreak a_{31}\right)u^{\gamma_{1}}w^{\gamma_{3}}+\left(\lambda_{2}a_{23}+a_{32}\right)v^{\gamma_{2}}w^{\gamma_{3}},\\ \widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{3}(S)\leq\left(\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}a_{13}+a_{31}\right)u^{\gamma_{1}}w^{\gamma_{3}}+\left(\lambda_{1}a_{12}+a_{21}\right)u^{\gamma_{1}}v^{\gamma_{2}}\lambda_{2}+\left(\lambda_{2}a_{23}+a_{32}\right)v^{\gamma_{2}}w^{\gamma_{3}}.\end{array}\right.

Therefore, in order for the following inequalities to be achieved (according to the non-negativity of each component of SS)

{𝒞~1​(S)≤0,𝒞~2​(S)≤0,𝒞~3​(S)≤0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{1}(S)\leq 0,\\ \widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{2}(S)\leq 0,\\ \widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{3}(S)\leq 0,\end{array}\right.

it is enough to verify that

{λ1​a12+a21≤0,λ1​a13+a31≤0,λ2​a13+a31≤0,λ2​a23+a32≤0,λ1​λ2​a13+a31≤0.\left\{\allowbreak\begin{array}[]{c}\allowbreak\lambda_{1}a_{12}+a_{21}\leq 0,\\ \allowbreak\lambda_{1}a_{13}+a_{31}\leq 0,\\ \lambda_{2}a_{13}+\allowbreak a_{31}\leq 0,\\ \lambda_{2}a_{23}+a_{32}\leq 0,\\ \lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}a_{13}+a_{31}\leq 0.\end{array}\right. (3.14)

So we distinguish two cases:

  • •

    When A∈𝒮​𝒦3×3−:A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{-}: It hold that ai​j≤0a_{ij}\leq 0 with i<ji<j, and ai​j+aj​i≤0a_{ij}+a_{ji}\leq 0, for i,j=1,2,3i,j=1,2,3. Consequently, choosing any values λ1,λ2>1\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>1 is sufficient to ensure that (3.14) is satisfied, and thus the assumption ( A 3). Hence, by applying Theorem 3, the desired result is established.

  • •

    When A∈𝒮​𝒦3×3+:A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{+}: It hold that ai​j≥0a_{ij}\geq 0 with i<ji<j, and ai​j+aj​i≤0a_{ij}+a_{ji}\leq 0, for i,j=1,2,3i,j=1,2,3. Consequently, choosing any values λ1,λ2<1\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}<1 is sufficient to ensure that (3.14) is satisfied, and thus the assumption ( A 3). Hence, By invoking Theorem 4, the desired result is established.

This completes the proof. ∎

Remark 2.

If the diffusion coefficients differ from each other, the question of whether system (3.11) possesses global classical solutions(with or without uniform-in-time bounds) or undergoes blow-up remains open, in the following cases:

  • •

    When γi=1\gamma_{i}=1 for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3, and A∈𝒮​𝒦3×3\(𝒮​𝒦3×3−∪𝒮​𝒦3×3+)A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}\backslash\left(\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{-}\cup\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{+}\right), under the boundary condition (1.16) or (1.17).

  • •

    When γi>1\gamma_{i}>1 for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3, and A∈𝒮​𝒦3×3\(𝒮​𝒦3×3−∪𝒮​𝒦3×3+)A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}\backslash\left(\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{-}\cup\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}^{+}\right), under one of the boundary conditions (1.14)–(1.17).

  • •

    When γi≥1\gamma_{i}\geq 1 for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3, and A∈𝒮​𝒦3×3A\in\mathcal{SK}_{3\times 3}, under nonlinear boundary conditions.
